Title: Tranferring myself out of the game

Messages.Author: Mari
Messages.Body:
Hi all,

The group in Portland is currently playing a sealed-deck league which
is much fun. One of the fun things about it is the limited amount of
cards you get and the other is the fact that Unique Items, Locations,
Allies, Retainers, Vampires and other unique cards are permanently
burned if they are burned during a game (diablerized, Protect Thine
Own, Vulnerability, excess agg damage / Rampage, Arson, Unnatural
Disaster / Illegal Search and Seizure, Shattering Blow, Canine Hordes
etc.)

Anyhow, last night, my Theo Bell was put in torpor during my turn. I
told everyone that since I was dead anyhow (I had 3 pool, 1 ready
minion and a stealth bleed deck behind me), that I was going to
transfer myself out in order to save Theo Bell from the indignities
and permanency of diablerie. I was told that it was against the rules
to transfer myself out. I saw no way to gain any more VPs than I
currently had and was going to get ousted on my next turn (I had
stealth bleed behind me and zero intercept), so was I obligated to
stay in the game?

Back in June of 2001 there was this exchange - is it still valid?

Xian wrote:
> "Andrew S. Davidson" <a...@csi.com> wrote in message
> news:6E02ABFC0AF2D74B.896E35F7...@lp.airnews.net..
> > I can't see the Ravnos player's actions being open to question but
> > what about the Set player? Is transferring yourself out of the game
> > allowed by the new rule? He's clearly not trying to win but there's
> > little point in giving someone a loss for this as that's what he's
> > trying to achieve anyway.
>
> My personal interpretation (IANALSJ, of course...I can't remember if
> I've heard his opinion on this one.) is that transferring out could
> conceivably be disallowed/looked upon unfavorably by the new rule.
> Again, this is something that I'm not sure on myself. I'd probably
> issue a caution, and tell them to make sure it didn't happen again, as
> it's unsportsmanlike.

If you cannot gain any more VPs, transferring out is as reasonable an
alternative as anything else.

--
LSJ (vte...@white-wolf.com) V:TES Net.Rep for White Wolf, Inc.

We went with a more RPG definition of what gets burned... Horrid
Reality and Illusions of the Kindred are both illusory effects,
therefore the "real" items/minions wouldn't have been burned, so the
item/minions is not burned from the league. Also, retainers,
equipment, locations or other unique cards (Tasha Morgan, JS Simmons,
Sengir Dagger, The Rack etc.)that are on minions who get burned have
to be specifically targeted to be considered burned from the league
(i.e. a minion with Tasha getting diablerized does not mean Tasha is
burned. If the minion with Tasha is in combat and someone decides to
move to long and target Tasha with a gun, then Tasha is burned from
the league)

into it, but if they were around, i'm sure we'd figure something out.

> of "unique")?

Giants Blood running around - but Muaziz is definitely unique and you

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Mari wrote:

> I was told that it was against the rules
> to transfer myself out.

It is not. You can transfer yourself out whenever you want to. In tournament
play, you are required to play such that you maximize your victory, but if
you are at 3 pool and have only vampires in torpor, maximizing your victory
is getting out of the game as soon as possible.

That you are using funky house rules (i.e. if Theo is deablerized, he is
permanently out of the league) only makes it even more in your best interest
to oust yourself.

> play, you are required to play such that you maximize your victory, but if
> you are at 3 pool and have only vampires in torpor, maximizing your victory
> is getting out of the game as soon as possible.
>

In spite of knowing the official rules, many people consider this
unsportsmanlike (meaning, they don't like it when someone does this).
The reason is very simple: people are expected to work hard to win. If
someone's prey simply decides to call it quits, the others feel he's
being favored. Strangely, this doesn't always hold true for the
predator role. People aren't as bothered that someone's predator isn't
putting pressure on him, probably because this happens more often.
This is the way most people *feel*, anyway (there's no such thing in
the rules).
If there's a valid reason to oust oneself, however, this might
change. Were you referring to the case where your minions were
graverobbed? Even so, this won't benefit you directly.
I really don't see a *reason* to oust yourself other than the
need to get a smoke or something. I only see no reasons not to, save
the fact that since "having no hopes of gaining more than X VPs" is
somewhat subjective, this might raise suspicions of collusion. IMHO,
it should be avoided.

Thanks,
David Pontes

> unsportsmanlike (meaning, they don't like it when someone does this).

The basis of the question is that any action the person takes results
in a loss. It follows then that any "work" that the player does is
"working" toward a loss. You cannot "play to win" if every available
option for play open to you doesn't lead to a win.

If you throw away the basis (and use a different basis, one in which the
player in question has an option available that leads to the accumulation
of more VPs), then the answer is very different.

--

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
On Thu, 19 Sep 2002, LSJ wrote:

> The basis of the question is that any action the person takes results
> in a loss. It follows then that any "work" that the player does is
> "working" toward a loss. You cannot "play to win" if every available
> option for play open to you doesn't lead to a win.

But the answer to the question, as it is commonly given, implies some
certain knowledge of future events that does not exist. The best you can
do is assess those odds, as things stand at that moment. Cross-table
rescues and votes called by other players that generate pool are two
common examples of play that can nullify whatever filegreed pile of
if-thens you've got in your head. I've transferred myself out in the
past, but I don't think I was technically playing to win at that point. I
certainly *felt* like my game was over, but I didn't *know* it was. And
if we accept that feeling as being sufficient, then it isn't really any
standard at all.

David Cherryholmes

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
David Cherryholmes wrote:
>
> On Thu, 19 Sep 2002, LSJ wrote:
>
> > The basis of the question is that any action the person takes results
> > in a loss. It follows then that any "work" that the player does is
> > "working" toward a loss. You cannot "play to win" if every available
> > option for play open to you doesn't lead to a win.
>
> But the answer to the question, as it is commonly given, implies some
> certain knowledge of future events that does not exist.

No. The question expressly states that knowledge as a given fact. The
answer doesn't change that.

If the knowledge that you cannot gain more VPs doesn't exist, then
it follows that there is some way for you to gain more VPs.

> The best you can
> do is assess those odds, as things stand at that moment. Cross-table
> rescues and votes called by other players that generate pool are two
> common examples of play that can nullify whatever filegreed pile of
> if-thens you've got in your head. I've transferred myself out in the
> past, but I don't think I was technically playing to win at that point. I
> certainly *felt* like my game was over, but I didn't *know* it was. And
> if we accept that feeling as being sufficient, then it isn't really any
> standard at all.

I wasn't suggesting that one accept the feeling. I was, as I have done
in the past, answering the question as given. The question as given
stated that there was no way to gain more VPs. It didn't state how
that knowledge came to be obtained - it simply stated the condition
as a fact.

As I've often said, it is nearly impossible to be in a truly "lost"
position (except for the moments leading up to your ousting).

But, if you wish to introduce "feelings", then, if the judge likes,
he can use "reasonable" in there - if the player wishes to do X and
cannot reasonably (in the judge's determination) gain more VPs by
doing something else, then she is free to do X.

Paul Steiner writes:
> Is it ever possible to know that

>additional VP.

One stunt you could do to prevent your
grandprey from transferring out would be
to offer to let him withdraw once he's your
prey if some unlikely event happens. You
could bring 5 regular dice, roll them once he
becomes your prey, and
if they all come up sixes, you'll let him leave.
He then has a 1 in 7776 chance of getting
a 1/2 VP; incredibly slim, but a verifiable chance,
so he shouldn't legally be allowed to withdraw.
You can make the deal if there's any benefit
to you to him trying to stay, as your expected
loss is so slim.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)
"It is better to be wrong than to be vague" - Freeman Dyson

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
CurtAdams wrote:
>
> Paul Steiner writes:

>
> One stunt you could do to prevent your
> grandprey from transferring out would be
> to offer to let him withdraw once he's your
> prey if some unlikely event happens. You
> could bring 5 regular dice, roll them once he
> becomes your prey, and
> if they all come up sixes, you'll let him leave.
> He then has a 1 in 7776 chance of getting
> a 1/2 VP; incredibly slim, but a verifiable chance,
> so he shouldn't legally be allowed to withdraw.
> You can make the deal if there's any benefit
> to you to him trying to stay, as your expected
> loss is so slim.

Attempting to use hard numbers for probabilities is
not advisable in these situations, since the hard
numbers are impossible to come by.

For example, the above fails to account for the
probability that the player would be Life Booned if
she went ahead and transferred out. Even if it
did, that probability would then have to be adjusted
by the expected VPs the player would get in that
event. Even if you got that far, you would not then
compare that number with the 1/7776 figure above -
the latter fails to take into account the probability
that either you or she (or both) are ousted before
you become her predator and she exhausts her library
/and/ fails to consider the odds of someone else
thwarting her withdrawal if you get that far.

If the judge is omniscient enough to evaulate such
odds numerically for the given situation, then he
should feel free to make rulings based on the hard
numbers. (i.e., You can expect a GW 6503 out of
13772024831 times with that play, which is better
than with any other play, so you must make that play).

If not, then he should make rulings based on
reasonable expectations.

The Life Boon thing addresses that point:

The prey has a small chance if she doesn't transfer out (as you
say) *and* has a small chance if she *does* transfer out (since
she could then be Life Booned and go on to accumulate more VPs).

If the judge rules that the chances are negligible in either event,
the prey is free to choose either method as she wishes.
